doc.title: George Shearing interviewed by Joe Williams, New York City, New York, March 8, 1996

title: The all-blind band: Lunceford charts in Braille and the lost glass eye
summary: Shearing says he was brought up on Jimmie Lunceford, describes the 1937 all-blind band with Braille scores and leader Claude Bampton, tells the glass-eye story and Benny Carter hearing the recording.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: I was brought up on Jimmy Lunceford.
There was an all blind band in 1937. Fifteen musicians. Fifteen blind guys, taught to be musicians, from being chair caners, basket makers—
They caned chairs. They made baskets, and they were taught to play instruments and be musicians. And the scores were done in Braille. We had Lunceford’s “Stratosphere,” Benny Carter’s “Night Fall.”
Did you have his suite too?

Yeah, we had all the Braille charts. And I’m the only one that didn’t need it, and I’d pick it up by ear right away. The theme song for the band by the way was “I’ll See You In My Dreams.” And the only fully sighted man was a man named Claude Bampton, who was a kind of semi-professional band leader in England. He had this huge baton, you know whit, whit, whit, [sings] “I’ll See You In My Dreams.” One night, you know blind people always have to set up in a theater a little bit earlier than the sighted. It takes us a bit longer. And Claude said, “Okay fellas, you ready?” One guy said, “No, just a minute, I
lost my eye.” His glass eye had fallen out, rolled across the stage, and there was 15 blind guys down on the floor—
I kid you not, this is the God’s honest truth. Fifteen blind guys down on the floor looking for this eye.

They found it. And they didn’t massacre it at all, they found it. He put it in. Whit, whit, whit — “I’ll See You In —” One night as a matter of fact, we were at Benny Carter’s house for dinner. And I had a tape recorder with me. And I had a recording of the band, the all-blind band playing “Night Fall.” And he says, “Who is that?” I said, “Well you know the tune, don’t you?” “Yeah.” So I explained to him about the all-blind band. So I guess you know there was, jazz came into England and we copy.
But you went on to innovation though you know. You went from assimilation to innovation.
